front.title: Retransmission Indication for IS-IS Fast Flooding

abstract.t: defines a Flooding Parameters TLV that allows an IS-IS node to advertise, among other things, a Receive Window (RWIN) that bounds the number of unacknowledged Link State PDUs (LSPs) a neighbor may have outstanding, and an LSPs-per-PSNP (LPP) threshold that triggers immediate acknowledgment. In practice these two mechanisms -- a credit-based flow-control window and an acknowledgment cadence -- are the parts of that are most important, useful, and likely to be implemented at scale; the sender-side congestion-control algorithms described in that document are described only as optional, local choices, without a single mandatory algorithm.

A credit-based window alone does not signal congestion: as long as acknowledgments keep freeing credit, a sender may keep refilling the window up to RWIN even while it is actively retransmitting LSPs on that adjacency. Without an explicit, mandatory-to-implement reaction to observed retransmission, fast flooding at scale can degenerate into sustained retransmission storms instead of converging.

This document specifies that a node SHOULD halve the effective outstanding-LSP ceiling it uses against a neighbor's advertised RWIN whenever the number of LSP retransmissions it has generated toward that neighbor within a trailing time window exceeds a configured threshold. This local backoff applies unconditionally, regardless of whether it is signaled to, or understood by, the neighbor. This document additionally defines a lightweight Retransmission (RTX) indication, carried as a new flag in the existing Flags sub-TLV of the Flooding Parameters TLV, that a node sets while it is in this condition. Advertising the RTX flag lets the neighbor, in turn, adjust its own advertised RWIN so that the adjacency converges toward a stable operating point at the highest speed it can sustain, without either side needing prior knowledge of the other's or the link's characteristics.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: ("IS-IS Fast Flooding") introduces the Flooding Parameters TLV to let IS-IS neighbors negotiate faster and more efficient Link State PDU (LSP) flooding. Of the sub-TLVs it defines, two provide the practical basis for flow control that implementations are expected to deploy at scale:

ul.li: The Receive Window (RWIN) sub-TLV (), which bounds the number of unacknowledged LSPs a sender may have outstanding toward a given neighbor ().
The LSPs-per-PSNP (LPP) sub-TLV (), which sets the number of unacknowledged LSPs that triggers an immediate PSNP rather than waiting for the periodic PSNP timer ().

section.t: RWIN is, by design, a flow-control mechanism: it prevents a sender from overrunning a receiver's buffering capacity, but it says nothing about whether the path or the receiver is currently congested. A sender that naively refills its outstanding-LSP count up to RWIN as soon as acknowledgments arrive will do so even while some of those acknowledgments are arriving late enough to have already triggered retransmission timers. Sustained retransmissions are direct evidence of loss or of a receiver falling behind, yet leaves the reaction to that evidence as an unspecified, optional, sender-local congestion-control algorithm ().

Experience indicates that if that reaction is not made mandatory in some minimal form, it will not be consistently implemented, and the fast flooding rates enabled by can make things worse, not better, under loss or overload: nodes keep sending at the full advertised window and retransmission storms are sustained rather than damped. This document closes that gap without requiring a full congestion-window algorithm. It specifies that a node SHOULD locally reduce its effective sending ceiling relative to RWIN whenever it is retransmitting, independent of any signaling, and it defines a single-bit Retransmission (RTX) indication, carried in the existing Flags sub-TLV (), that additionally lets a neighbor observing the indication tune its own RWIN (and, optionally, LPP) advertisement toward a stable value that sustains the highest speed the adjacency can support without further retransmission.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Motivation
section.t: Consider a point-to-point adjacency where the receiver has advertised RWIN=60 and LPP=15, as suggested in . The sender transmits LSPs up to its outstanding-LSP ceiling, which absent any other information it sets to RWIN. If the receiver becomes momentarily overloaded, its PSNPs are delayed, the sender's retransmit timers fire (as governed by minimumLSPTransmissionInterval ), and the sender retransmits. Because retransmitted LSPs are, from the point of view of the credit-window bookkeeping, simply outstanding LSPs like any other, the sender has no built-in reason to reduce the number of LSPs it keeps outstanding: as soon as any acknowledgment (even a late one) arrives and frees credit, it refills up to RWIN again.

This is workable at the flooding rates for which 's historical defaults were designed, but it is precisely the failure mode that fast flooding at larger scale must avoid: a receiver that falls behind by a small margin can be kept continuously on the edge of retransmission by a sender that never backs off, which in turn keeps generating the retransmissions that caused the problem in the first place. A minimal, mandatory-to-honor local backoff at the sender -- halving the outstanding-LSP ceiling whenever the sender's rate of LSP retransmissions toward that neighbor exceeds a configured threshold, regardless of whether that condition is signaled -- is sufficient to break this cycle without requiring implementations to build and tune a separate congestion-control algorithm. Signaling that condition to the neighbor additionally lets the advertised RWIN itself be tuned toward the correct steady-state value for the current link and peer, rather than being fixed forever at a conservative, offline-computed default chosen without knowledge of either.

A single halving step is not guaranteed to be enough. If the mismatch between the ceiling the sender was using and what the receiver and path can actually sustain is larger than a factor of two, the sender may continue retransmitting even after backing off once. It is therefore highly desirable that the receiver, on seeing the RTX indication, actively squelch its own advertised RWIN rather than merely holding it steady: a lower advertised RWIN gives the sender a lower base to halve against, and, since the RTX flag persists for as long as retransmission continues, this can repeat over successive rounds until a stable point is reached where retransmission stops. Symmetrically, once retransmission has stopped, the window should be reopened again, but deliberately more slowly than it was closed, so that the adjacency settles into a stable operating point instead of oscillating between overload and underuse (see ).

section.name: The RTX Flag
section.t: This document defines a new bit in the Flags sub-TLV of the Flooding Parameters TLV , called the RTX flag (bit TBD1, suggested value 1; bit 0 is the existing O-flag defined in ).

A node maintains, per adjacency, a count of the LSP retransmissions it has generated toward the neighbor within a trailing retransmission window of locally configured duration. It sets the RTX flag on that adjacency when this count exceeds a locally configured retransmission threshold, and clears the flag once the count falls back to or below the threshold. As with other Flooding Parameters TLV state, the flag is advertised in IIHs and PSNPs () and reflects the most recently advertised value until updated.

Both the retransmission window and the retransmission threshold are local matters, not signaled to the neighbor, and implementations SHOULD make them configurable. A window on the order of a few times the adjacency's round-trip acknowledgment time, and a threshold on the order of a small number of retransmissions (e.g., 3), are reasonable starting points: they are short and low enough to react promptly to sustained loss, yet high enough that a single, isolated retransmission does not by itself set the flag or trigger the backoff of .

When the RTX flag transitions from clear to set, or when a node reduces an RWIN or LPP value it advertises in reaction to the RTX flag (), the node SHOULD send an IIH carrying the updated Flags, Receive Window, and LSPs-per-PSNP sub-TLVs immediately, rather than waiting for its next regularly scheduled Hello: the sooner a neighbor learns of the condition, the sooner it can stop sustaining it by squelching its own advertised RWIN. Neither nor defines an IIH sent outside the periodic Hello schedule for this purpose; doing so here is additional behavior recommended by this document and does not replace the regularly scheduled IIHs.

By contrast, when the RTX flag clears, or when a node widens an RWIN or LPP value it had previously reduced, no equivalent urgency applies: the updated value SHOULD simply be carried in the next regularly scheduled IIH or PSNP. This asymmetry is intentional and mirrors the deliberately slow reopening described in : there is no benefit to rushing the good news, and doing so would only invite oscillation.

The RTX flag is advertised so that a neighbor can tune its own RWIN (and, optionally, LPP) advertisement toward a stable operating point, as described in . It is not what triggers the sending node's own backoff: that backoff, described in , is local and unconditional, and applies whether or not the RTX flag is advertised or understood by the neighbor.

section.name: Sender Behavior (Local Backoff)
section.t: Whenever the retransmission threshold defined in is exceeded on a given adjacency -- i.e., the node's own local trigger for setting the RTX flag on that adjacency is met -- it SHOULD halve the effective outstanding-LSP ceiling it uses on that adjacency, relative to the RWIN value currently advertised by the neighbor, rather than continuing to refill up to the full RWIN as acknowledgments arrive. This behavior is local and unconditional: it applies regardless of whether the node advertises the RTX flag, and regardless of whether the neighbor understands it, so that an adjacency to a peer that does not implement this document still benefits from the backoff. The exact reduction is a local matter; a simple halving is sufficient to convert sustained retransmission into a self-damping condition without the bookkeeping of a full congestion window ().

A single halving step is not guaranteed to stop retransmission by itself. If the neighbor also reduces its advertised RWIN in response to the RTX indication (), the sender halves its ceiling again relative to that newly reduced value the next time its retransmission count again exceeds the threshold, and so on for as long as the condition persists. See for how this repeated, mutual reduction is expected to converge, and for how the ceiling is subsequently reopened.

section.name: Receiver Behavior (RWIN Convergence)
section.t: A node observing that a neighbor has set the RTX flag toward it SHOULD treat this as feedback that the RWIN (and, if used, LPP) value it currently advertises to that neighbor exceeds what the neighbor and the path between them can sustain, and SHOULD actively squelch its advertised RWIN and/or LPP accordingly (, ), rather than merely leaving the advertisement unchanged and waiting for the sender's own backoff to be sufficient. It SHOULD advertise the reduced value immediately, as described in , rather than waiting for its next regularly scheduled IIH.

Because the RTX flag remains set for as long as the neighbor keeps retransmitting, a single reduction is not guaranteed to be enough: if the flag is still set after the receiver's next opportunity to re-advertise the Flooding Parameters TLV, it SHOULD reduce its advertised RWIN further (e.g., halving it again), and repeat this on each subsequent round for as long as the flag remains set. Combined with the sender's own halving (), this mutual, repeated reduction converges geometrically to a stable operating point at which retransmission ceases, without either node needing prior knowledge of the other's or the link's characteristics.

section.name: Convergence and Hysteresis
section.t: The mechanisms of and are deliberately asymmetric: closing the window, on either side, is fast and multiplicative (halving), while reopening it is slow and incremental. Once the RTX flag has cleared, a receiver MAY probe for a higher sustainable RWIN, and a sender MAY correspondingly raise its effective ceiling toward the newly advertised RWIN, but both SHOULD do so in small steps over successive rounds rather than jumping back to the prior value immediately. An immediate, full restoration would likely reproduce the original overload and cause the RTX flag to be set again on the very next round, oscillating between overload and underuse instead of settling.

This fast-close/slow-open hysteresis is what allows the repeated, mutual squeezing described in and to actually converge and then hold at a stable point close to the highest speed the adjacency can sustain, rather than merely oscillating between a too-fast state that retransmits and a too-slow state that immediately reopens back into retransmission.

The steps of the slow reopening are, per , ordinarily carried on regularly scheduled IIHs rather than triggered immediately. If a node's configured Hello interval is long, relying solely on that periodic cadence could make reopening -- and hence recovery of full flooding speed -- impractically slow even after the condition that caused the squeeze is long gone. In that case, a node SHOULD instead pace the reopening steps using a separate timer dedicated to this purpose, decoupled from the Hello interval, so that the rate of reopening can be chosen independently of how infrequently Hellos are otherwise exchanged. This timer only paces the sending of the already-slow, incremental widening steps of this section; it does not apply to the fast-close case, which remains governed by .

section.name: Interaction with RFC 9681
section.t: This document does not change the encoding, semantics, or use of the RWIN or LPP sub-TLVs defined in ; it only adds a bit to the existing Flags sub-TLV and defines recommended behavior that references those existing sub-TLVs. Nodes that do not implement this document continue to interoperate exactly as described in ; the RTX flag is simply unset (or ignored, if received from a neighbor that implements it and this one does not).

This document intentionally does not modify or replace the sender-side congestion control algorithms of or ; an implementation that already implements one of those algorithms MAY treat the RTX flag purely as an additional congestion signal within that algorithm, in place of, or in addition to, the sender-local backoff of .

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document reuses the Flooding Parameters TLV and its authentication properties defined in ; the security considerations of that document () apply unchanged.

A false or forged RTX indication has similar consequences to a forged RWIN or LPP value discussed in : an attacker able to inject a spoofed indication on an adjacency could induce a neighbor to needlessly reduce its RWIN, slowing convergence, or could suppress a legitimate indication to prevent a peer from backing off. Both require the same link-layer access already assumed by , and the impact is bounded to the affected adjacency and is self-correcting once the RTX flag state is next advertised truthfully.
